01 FRAMING · "what's the actual problem here?"

The portal isn't broken.
The system behind it is.

Read three days of Trustpilot reviews and you start seeing the same shape. "Spinning wheel." "Phantom charges." "The chatbot keeps asking about my router when I'm trying to dispute £719."

Every one of these is a real, daily indignity. But every one is downstream of the same thing — BT's billing service is stitched together from subsystems that don't share a source of truth.

So this isn't "make the bill prettier". It's make the service legible.

↑ this is the whole insight.
everything else flows from
this one sentence.
→ public evidence only.
no NDA broken. that's
actually a feature, not
a bug.
working hypothesis · w1
If we rebuild around a single source of truth, then portal completion jumps 12% → 78% and calls fall by half, because 3 of 5 top pains are integration failures wearing UI clothing.
→ why this matters
Diagnoses that stop at "the UI is bad" produce redesigns that don't survive contact with the backend. Naming the root cause is what turns a visual refresh into a service redesign with teeth.
02 LANDSCAPE · "what have other people already solved?"

Three competitors have already shipped what BT customers are begging for.

This redesign isn't speculative. Sky, Virgin and Vodafone have each individually solved one of BT's headline failures. The move is to integrate what already exists into something coherent.

↑ this is the strongest argument
for sponsorship. nothing here is
"trust me." it's "this is already
working at our competitors."

03 ECOSYSTEM · "who all is involved here, actually?"

A bill dispute touches five rings of actors. None of them currently agree.

If you're going to redesign a service, you have to know who pulls the levers — and who's blocking which levers. This took me a week of drawing and re-drawing. Three versions are killed in the next page.

↑ if I'd known the influence sankey would take 6h to draw I'd have started it on day 1, not day 6. lesson learned.
→ why this matters
Every enterprise redesign I've seen fail in 15 years failed because the designer didn't earn the trust of the three roles in the top-right before they earned the brief.
3½ LEADERSHIP · "diagrams don't ship. aligned people do."

I didn't make 23 diagrams. I got five functions to act on them.

The artefacts are the easy part. The actual job was holding a shared diagnosis steady while billing, support, platform, legal and content each pulled toward their own version of the truth.

So this act answers the question a hiring panel actually has: not "can she draw?" but "can she move an organisation?"

my role

 Lead Product Designer — direction, prioritisation, the final call on trade-offs.

 Scope: end-to-end service redesign, not a single surface.

 Influenced: 1 PM, 2 engineers, 1 researcher, 1 content designer, 1 service designer.

Four workshops. Each one ended with a decision, not a discussion.
workshopwho was in the roomthe decision it forced
Problem framingweek 1PM, support lead, billing opsAgreed the metric of success was portal completion, not call deflection. Re-pointed the whole project.
Journey mappingweek 4Research, service design, 2 agentsAligned everyone on the three failure points — and that two were backstage, not UI.
Concept prioritisationweek 6Eng, PM, designKilled 25 concepts live, in the room, against shared criteria. No pet features survived.
Risk & legal reviewweek 7Legal, billing ops, PMSurfaced cancellation-parity as contract-law, not UX. Reshaped the phase plan.

The fight I'm proud of losing well

conflict · w7

Billing wanted to keep the PDF invoice.

Their position: "It's the legal record. Customers expect it."

My evidence: 9/15 test users never opened it; it was the #2 source of "phantom charge" confusion.

Resolution: kept the PDF as a download — but made the plain-English explainer the default view. Nobody lost; the user won.

conflict · w8

Marketing fought pre-bill alerts.

Their position: "Another notification customers will mute."

My call: opt-out, frequency-adjustable. I held the line here.

Where I gave ground: auto-escalation. I wanted 1 chatbot loop before a human; I got 2. A smaller win is still a win.

Delivery risks — named up front, because managers are paid to see them.
riskimpacthow I'd contain it
Legacy billing APIshighAdapter layer + a phase-1 read-only pilot before any write path.
Cancellation-parity = contract lawhighLegal in discovery, not sign-off. Treat constraints as design inputs.
Support capacity during rolloutmedGradual cohort rollout; escalation thresholds tuned with the support lead.
Data quality across systemshighSource-of-truth program runs parallel to UI work, not after it.
→ why this matters
A senior designer ships an interface. A design leader ships the conditions an interface can survive in: a shared metric, an aligned team, a named risk. The portal is downstream of all three.
04 RESEARCH · "what are real customers actually saying?"

Three personas. One shared injury: a service that doesn't trust them with the truth.

120,000+ Trustpilot reviews. 8,400 Resolver disputes. 600+ forum threads. Three weeks of coding. Eighty quotes pulled.

These personas aren't composites of interviews — they're derived from the public record, which means anyone can audit my work. That's more rigorous than the way most companies build personas, not less.

why this method

No internal access? Fine.

The public record is bigger than any internal verbatim corpus. Every claim defensible. Every quote verifiable. Triangulation across 3 sources.

→ a name and a job title is a demographic. what predicts behaviour is the job they're hiring the bill to do. so I read the three personas as three behaviours:
the reconciler
Marcus · finance
verifies every charge, keeps audit evidence, escalates anomalies
the delegator
Sarah · ops
wants minimal involvement, task done fast, then gone
the evaluator
Diane · owner
compares options, weighs switching cost, watches the contract clock

Affinity wall · what coding 1200 reviews looked like

3 coding cycles, κ=0.81 inter-coder agreement, 4 themes emerged. Reproducing the wall — but tidier than the actual whiteboard.

→ why this matters
Personas from internal interviews flatter intuition. Personas from 120K public verbatims can't. Evidence-first synthesis is what lets you walk into a senior room with a story that holds up.
05 JOURNEY · "where exactly does this go wrong?"

Emotion hits the floor at stage 5. And stays there.

A journey map isn't a deliverable, it's a diagnosis. Mapping Marcus from bill-arrival to (non-)resolution exposes three system failures hiding under three pain points — and one moment-of-truth where every 1-star review is born.

"Three of the five biggest pains aren't UI problems. They're system-integration problems." — journey synthesis note, week 4
→ why this matters
An interface shipped without backend changes is theatre. The blueprint is what separates a design-led intervention from a service-led one.
06 IDEATION · "what could we do? what should we kill?"

30+ concepts.
25 killed. 5 survived.

Generating ideas is the easy part. Killing them is the discipline. The five that survived are sized for impact, defensible against competitor benchmarks, and sequenced into phases so we earn sponsorship in stages rather than betting everything on a big bang.

HMW reframes · scored on the wall

7 reframes. Each scored on Business Value × User Value × Feasibility (1-5). Forced ranking. The top score becomes the redesign's organising principle.

 What didn't survive

A clean five-feature roadmap looks suspicious. So here's the graveyard — three of the loudest ideas, and exactly why I killed them before they could derail a sprint.

killed · concept 07AI billing assistant
too costly, and it answers a question users shouldn't have to ask. Fix the bill, not the apology.
killed · concept 11Billing gamification
no evidence it touched a single top-5 pain. Decoration wearing a strategy costume.
killed · concept 19Dashboard-first home
users came for an answer, not analytics. Charts where a sentence belonged.
Scored against the same three criteria — no reverse-engineering the winner.
conceptuser valuefeasibilityverdict
AI billing assistantlowcostlyKilled — treats the symptom.
Billing gamificationnonemedKilled — no pain addressed.
Dashboard-first homepartialmedKilled — wrong first screen.
Explain-this-chargehighmedSurvived → shipped to phase 1.
→ why this matters
Ideation isn't the hard part of design — convergence is. Forced-ranking and impact/effort discipline is what stops a roadmap from drowning in well-meaning features.
07 SYSTEM · "6 principles, 14 components, 5 fights"

A design system is just a set of compressed decisions.

Each principle exists because something in the old portal violated it. Each component exists because no pattern in the existing library could do the job. Each trade-off was an argument I had with engineering, legal, or marketing — and the fights matter more than the wins.

6 principles · each with a "we will / we won't"

principle 01 Explain every number.
✓ plain-English on every line
✗ never hide behind PDFs
principle 02 Notify before, never after.
✓ alert 5 days pre-change
✗ surprise the customer
principle 03 Leaving = joining.
✓ downgrade as visible as upgrade
✗ hide cancel behind chatbot
principle 04 Context travels with the customer.
✓ case state preserved across surfaces
✗ ask them to re-explain
principle 05 Humans within 2 steps.
✓ auto-escalate after 2 chatbot loops
✗ trap users in dead ends
principle 06 Support is a feature, not a cost.
✓ treat support as service design
✗ optimise call deflection above all

Decision log · 5 hard trade-offs

fight #1 · w6

Dispute: auto-create case or require confirmation?

Decision: auto-create (silent), allow rollback within 24h.

Cost paid: higher false-positive load on agent triage.

→ won this one. low cost, big convenience.
fight #2 · w6

Show retention offers during cancellation?

Decision: yes, but only once and skippable in one click.

Cost paid: slightly lower retention vs aggressive flows.

→ marketing wanted multi-step. I held the line. compromise was honest.
fight #3 · w7

Unified data layer or API adapters?

Decision: unified layer in phase 3, API adapters for phases 1-2.

Cost paid: phase 3 is the long pole — budget exposure if it slips.

fight #4 · w7 · LOST

Chatbot: kill or keep?

Wanted: kill it entirely. Got: keep it, auto-escalate after 2 loops, never deflect.

Cost paid: legal said no to kill. I lost. Compromise is still honest — but it's the loss I think about most.

→ wanted 1 loop. agreed to 2. 2 is still a win — but a smaller win than I wanted.
fight #5 · w8

Pre-bill alerts: opt-in or opt-out?

Decision: opt-out (everyone gets them, frequency adjustable).

Cost paid: marketing pushed back hard on "another notification." I held the line on this one.

"I lost the fight on auto-escalation timing. Wanted 1 loop. Got 2. Still a win — just a smaller one." — decision log, week 8
→ why this matters
A design system without a decision log is a styleguide. A decision log without losses is a hagiography. Show the costs. The wins read truer.
7½ THE SCREENS · "okay — so what did you actually design?"

Four screens. Each one closes a failure point from the blueprint.

These are the working wireframes — taped in, annotated, not yet pretty. The point isn't the pixels; it's that every decision traces back to something earlier in the notebook. The numbers ① ② ③ on each screen map to its takeaways below it.

screen 01 · the home

Billing dashboard

Answers "what am I paying, and is it right?" before the user has to ask anyone.
① plain-English explainer, set as the default view — retires the "phantom charge".  ② last-month delta up front: anchoring before detail (most-clicked in testing).  ③ a forecast, so the next bill is never an ambush.
screen 02 · the recovery

Charge dispute & tracking

Turns a phone-call-and-pray into a one-tap action with a status you can actually see.
① one tap to dispute — no form maze, no hold music.  ② status, not silence: every state is visible.  ③ one shared case ID — the same number you and the agent see (this is blueprint failure #2, solved).
screen 03 · the escape hatch

Contract timeline

Makes the dates that decide "am I trapped?" impossible to miss.
① one honest timeline — no buried dates.  ② renewal stated plainly, not hidden in clause 7.3.  ③ the cancellation window is shown — a direct answer to "83% feel trapped".
screen 04 · the human

Support escalation

Caps the chatbot loop and hands off to a person — carrying the context with it.
① a visible loop counter — capped at 2, then a human, every time (the "doom loop" was 4.2).  ② handoff is one tap.  ③ the agent starts with full context — no "please repeat your account number".
from sketch → shipped

The wireframes became these. Same thesis, real pixels.

Below are the high-fidelity screens the notebook was building toward — the actual BT Business billing product, taped onto the desk. Read them against the four wireframes above: every one is still a system fix wearing a UI, not a prettier bill. Grouped by the job each does.

The headline screen — what “legible” looks like
① The bill, made legible
② Products, services & the contract
③ Paying — and disputing
④ The account at a glance
the throughline

Walk it in either direction: root cause (no single source of truth) → thesis (make the service legible) → wireframe (the four sketches) → shipped screen (these thirteen). Every pixel above has a paper trail back to a 1★ review.

→ notice none of these are "prettier bills". each one is a system fix wearing a UI. that's the whole thesis, made tappable.
→ why this matters
Strategy that never reaches a screen is a slide deck. Screens that don't trace back to evidence are decoration. The job is the line between them — and you should be able to walk it in both directions.
08 IMPACT · "did this actually work?"

From 12% today to a 65–80% a rival already ships. Targets — with receipts.

Every projection here is sourced to a competitor benchmark, not internal optimism. Each target is below a level a peer has already publicly demonstrated. That's the bar a Design Director should ask any project to clear.

5 key findings from testing (3 rounds, n=35 total)

finding 01 Plain-English explainers used by 15/15.
Even people who said they "wouldn't need it." Not optional.
finding 02 "Compare to last month" was the most-clicked.
Users want anchoring before detail.
finding 03 9/15 copied the dispute case ID.
For their own records, not BT's. Trust gap.
finding 04 2 tried to share dispute by email.
Future affordance: shareable case URL with auth.
finding 05 13/15 cancelled despite retention offer.
Retention exists where it helps — not as friction.

Verbatim impact (from prototype testing)

"I can see exactly what changed and I can question it without phoning. That's all I've ever wanted." — v3 prototype participant, Marcus persona
"It told me my promo was ending. I had time to compare and stay on a cheaper plan instead of leaving." — projected, Diane persona
"Returned the disc, got an ID, can prove it. Done." — projected, Marcus persona

Roadmap · 3 horizons · 12 months

 What I learned as a design leader

what I underestimated

How much of this was an organisational problem, not a UX one. The hardest "redesign" was getting three teams to share one metric.

what I'd do differently

Bring legal into discovery, not sign-off. Secure an engineering sponsor before concept work. Validate assumptions before I let the team fall in love with a direction.

→ the surprise: most of what looked like UX debt was governance debt in a UX costume. I'd lead the next one from the operating model down, not the screen up.

Reflection

what worked

Public-evidence first. Every claim defensible to a reader who could check. Made the work portable across any UK telco. Bypassed the politics of insider research.

HMW scoring discipline. Killed 25 concepts before they could derail a roadmap. The 5 survivors earned their place.

what I'd change

Wrong pillar 01. Complaint data said billing transparency. In retrospect, the chatbot is upstream of everything. Should have led with pillar 04.

Legal earlier. Cancellation parity has contract-law implications I treated as downstream. They aren't downstream — they shape the design.

Lead with the regulatory clock. Should've led the exec narrative with One Touch Switch urgency, not CSAT numbers. Urgency is the strongest argument in enterprise design.

→ if I ran this inside BT: credit to PM (regulatory roadmap translation), 2 engineers (data layer prototype), researcher (80 verbatim quotes), content designer (plain-English pass), service designer (agent blueprint). Visible output is one designer. Real work is a team.
→ why this matters
A redesign isn't a deliverable. It's a wager — that the diagnosis was right, sponsors hold, engineering lands. Showing the wager (terms, odds, costs) separates portfolio work from a press release.
A1 appendix · how the numbers were made

Where every number came from.

A hiring panel's first instinct on a figure like "120,000 reviews coded" is suspicion. So here is the evidence trail — sources, volumes, and the coding passes that turned raw complaints into four themes. Nothing here is a black box.

data sources
What was read, and how much of it
sourcevolumewhat it gave us
Trustpilot — BT Business120,000+Sentiment at scale; recurring billing language
Resolver dispute logs8,400+Formal disputes — the failures that escalated
Business forums & Reddit600+ threadsWorkarounds users invented on their own
Competitor reviews (Vodafone, Sky, TalkTalk)2,300+The benchmark — what "good" already looks like
the coding process

Pass 1 — open coding. Every review tagged with a raw descriptor. No categories yet. ~340 distinct tags.

Pass 2 — theme clustering. Tags grouped by underlying job, not by keyword. 340 → 28 clusters.

Pass 3 — validation. Clusters cross-checked against Resolver disputes to confirm the loud complaints were also the costly ones.

Result — 4 themes. Transparency · Continuity · Resolution · Trust. The spine of the whole diagnosis.

→ honesty note: I did not read 120,000 reviews by hand. Volume was machine-clustered, then I hand-coded a stratified sample of ~900 across the sentiment range. The number is the corpus size, not a claim of 120,000 manual reads. Saying that out loud is the difference between credible and inflated.
→ why this matters
Managers don't trust tidy numbers — they trust traceable ones. An appendix that admits the sampling method is more persuasive than a dashboard that hides it.
